text: This pump looks perfectly still. It isn't. One part of it is vibrating fifty-eight and a half times a second, by less than a twentieth of a pixel. Nothing touched it. A handheld camera found it.
This is HumSight. It turns a slow-motion phone video into a grid of virtual vibration sensors, and tells you whether a machine has a real fault, or whether it was just your hand shaking.

Machines vibrate abnormally before they fail. Contact sensors catch that, but they are fitted one machine at a time, so many machines are never monitored. Video should help. But the classic trick, magnifying all motion in the video, also magnifies camera shake. Film handheld, and a healthy machine looks broken.

It's for maintenance technicians checking an unmonitored machine with the phone they already carry. Plant managers deciding which machines need a real sensor. Field engineers who need visual proof for a customer. And students learning frequency and aliasing on real video.

Here's the idea. We split the frame into patches, and every patch becomes a sensor. For each one, OpenCV 5 measures motion smaller than a twentieth of a pixel, frame by frame, and turns it into a frequency, an amplitude and a signal-to-noise ratio. One video, forty-eight sensors, nothing wired to the machine.

Then an agent decides what to measure next, based on what it just measured. On this clip, the whole frame moves about half a pixel at three and a half hertz. That's the hand, not the machine, so it removes the shake first. Underneath, a fifty-eight and a half hertz peak appears in one region only. It zooms in with a finer scan, magnifies just that band, and files a work order. Every number comes from OpenCV. The language model only picks the next step, and a guard rejects any number that no tool produced.

Here's how it runs on AWS. The web page is static, on GitHub Pages. When you press run, it calls a Lambda Function URL. Lambda, on arm64 Graviton, pulls the clip from S3, runs the OpenCV pipeline and the agent, writes the magnified video, heatmap and spectrum back to S3, and returns short-lived presigned links. The browser loads the results straight from S3, and uploads go straight to S3 too. The Gemini key sits in SSM Parameter Store, CloudWatch logs every run, and a budget caps the cost. Only compact numbers ever reach Gemini. Never video frames.
And it's live. This is the public endpoint answering: OpenCV 5 on aarch64. These are real Lambda invocations in CloudWatch, one per analysis.

Alarm. Localized vibration at fifty-eight and a half hertz, zero point zero four seven pixels, with the camera shake removed. In the magnified video, only the faulty region moves. The spectrum separates shake from fault, the heatmap shows where, and the activity log shows every decision with the measurement behind it. The work order is ready for a maintenance ticket.
Now the same clip through a fixed, magnify-everything pipeline. It reports a fault at three and a half hertz. That's the camera shake. Exactly the mistake HumSight is built to avoid.

Next, a one hundred thirty hertz fault filmed at two hundred forty frames per second. The camera is too slow to measure it honestly, so HumSight says Inconclusive, and asks for at least three hundred twenty-five frames per second.

We measured it. On twelve test clips, the agent was right twelve times out of twelve. The fixed pipeline, five, and six times it magnified the shake. Median frequency error: five thousandths of a hertz. We also ran the pipeline under COOL on a Graviton4 instance. It gave no meaningful speed-up, and we report that as measured.
HumSight is indicative, not a certified ISO measurement, and it says so on every report. It's a first screen that tells you which machine deserves a real sensor. See what your machines are humming.
